The preserve of hard workers for the best part of two centuries, the chore jacket is one of those garments that brings with it a reassuring sense of solidity.
We took our popular Five-Pocket Chore Jacket (so called because it is a counterpart to our Five-Pocket Trousers, not, as you may think, because of the number of pockets it has – it actually has six pockets) and had it made up in that most revered of working fabrics.
Crafted from a robust 12.6oz cotton duck, a tightly woven cotton fabric with two yarns in the warp and a single yarn in the weft for a smooth, plain weave less prone to tears, the name is derived from from the dutch word for cotton - ‘doek’ - and since 1899 has been used for sails, tents and, of course, workwear.
In doing so, we have created a piece of clothing with all the utility of a chore jacket – a surfeit of pockets; a comfortable, roomy shape – that will age and patinate beautifully over the years.
Finishing things off with classic copper rivets and you have an unbeatable everyday jacket, unmatched in its durability and timeless design. If you feel so inclined, you could even wear it to do your chores. It won’t let you down.

Our relaxed tapered cut jean made from our brand new 14oz broken twill selvedge denim. Broken twill denim was first used in 1964 by Wrangler as a solution for combatting leg twist. The process of weaving fabric in this method sees the combination of both right hand twill (RHT) and left hand twill (LHT) reversed every two warp ends, forming a zigzag-like pattern in the denim and resulting in no bias in either direction of the weave, therefore eliminating leg twist.

p-ironheart-10506460659978.d:
Our slim tapered cut jeans, made from 19oz left-hand twill selvedge denim. While most of our denim features a traditional right-hand twill weave — characterised by a diagonal grain running from the top-right to the bottom-left of the fabric — this “lefty” denim is woven in the opposite direction under very high tension. This creates one of our stiffest, most robust fabrics, with an intense indigo hue that tends to fade with higher contrast than looser weaves.
To create this darkened variation, we take a pair of standard IH-777S-19L jeans and steep the entire garment in black dye using a direct dyeing process. This stains the indigo denim and stitching, with the added bonus of removing all shrinkage from the fabric. A unique middle ground between our traditional indigo and black denims, over time the fabric will gradually fade with blue-tinged hues in high-wear areas.

Knitted in Wakayama on 1980’s loopwheel machines, the 5.5oz Loopwheel Crew Neck T-Shirt from UTILITEES is 100% combed yarn cotton and offers a soft and comfortable feel. This particular model has been dyed using traditional processes that date back to the stone age, with the dye pigment derived from iron oxide found in the soil in the Okayama region of Japan.
The hand-dyeing process itself is extensive and time-consuming. Firstly a plain white T-shirt is submerged into a vat of pigment dye and gently rubbed by hand to disperse the colour evenly. T-shirts are dyed individually, with each taking around 10 minutes. The garment is then left to dry naturally, before repeating these steps to ensure a strong colour.
Whilst maybe not as vivid or vibrant as some industrial dying techniques, the resulting colour offers a very pleasing hue, displaying slight contrasts in tone and subtle marbling throughout the garment. Creating these unique colourways really is a labour of love — no two T-shirts will ever look exactly the same, and we think that's a good thing!
